subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Monday: After reading a news story about leaked company data, Vijay, head of a small design agency, emailed the team: 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.' People nodded, a bit stunned.

Two weeks later: Deadlines were tight. Saurabh, a copywriter, quietly opened a personal account on a phone and pasted in a client's draft brief to get a rewrite. Others did the same and kept quiet; nobody wanted to be the one to tell Vijay.

Six weeks later: A client spotted a line in a document that matched text shared only in a private brief. Vijay learned that half the team had been using personal accounts with client files. At a meeting Vijay asked, 'Why didn't anyone tell me?' A designer answered, 'You said no. We still had deadlines.'

qa.a: It said, 'No AI tools of any kind, effective today.'

qa.q: What was Vijay afraid of when sending the email?
qa.a: Vijay was afraid of leaking company data, after reading a news story about a leak.

qa.q: What other approach could Vijay have used instead of a full ban?
qa.a: Vijay could have written a clear policy on approved tools and what data never goes in, so people had a safe way to work and no reason to hide it.

qa.q: How did the ban look to Saurabh and the others?
qa.a: It felt unworkable with deadlines pressing, so they used personal accounts quietly and stayed silent, since nobody wanted to tell Vijay.

grounding: Shows a manager forbidding all AI use out of fear, while staff quietly use personal accounts, creating hidden risk that a clear policy could have prevented.
